title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Long-SessionDegradation in Full-Duplex Speech Models

paper.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Long-Session Degradation in Full-Duplex Speech Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract End-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models enable natural, real-time spoken interactions with interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech.
Prior evaluations have assessed diverse interaction capabilities and identified some degradation patterns across conversational turns.
However, how model behavior evolves over extended sessions remains insufficiently understood.
In this work, we address this gap by systematically characterizing long-session degradation and developing efficient methods to mitigate it.
We introduce a closed-loop evaluation framework for long-session stability and apply it to several publicly available full-duplex speech models, revealing degradation over time in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To mitigate this degradation, we propose a self-distillation-based training framework for lightweight LoRA adaptation that improves long-session stability with a small amount of additional training.
We further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions in full detail while compressing older interaction history into key-value representations. We evaluate our methods on three models with distinct architectures, assessing long-session stability, information retention, and computational efficiency. Across all three models, we show that LoRA adaptation mitigates performance degradation over ten-minute sessions, while adding TRC extends these gains beyond the training session length and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%. sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Natural spoken conversation involves dynamic coordination between speakers. A listener may respond before an utterance ends, provide backchannels, or interrupt when necessary, rather than waiting for strictly separated turns. Conventional spoken dialogue systems, however, have largely followed a turn-based interaction scheme in which listening and speaking occur in separate stages. To bridge this gap, recent advances in full-duplex spoken dialogue modeling have enabled models to process incoming speech while simultaneously generating spoken responses ( Nguyen et al., 2023 ; Défossez et al., 2024 ) . Together, these advances support more fluid interactions that better reflect the dynamics of natural human conversation. Recent research has increasingly adopted end-to-end approaches to full-duplex spoken dialogue modeling ( Défossez et al., 2024 ; Roy et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) , with efforts to extend these models beyond natural conversational behaviors to support more sophisticated real-time interaction, including tool use and multimodal perception ( Cui et al., 2026 ; Balam et al., 2026 ) . These developments reflect a broader shift toward interactive assistants that can continuously perceive their surroundings, respond to users as situations unfold, and provide ongoing support during everyday activities or complex tasks. Realizing this vision requires models to sustain reliable interaction over extended periods, rather than merely performing well in isolated exchanges. Despite this growing emphasis on continuous interaction, long-session stability has received limited attention in the development of end-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has explicitly targeted long-session stability in end-to-end full-duplex models through dedicated training strategies or architectural designs. Furthermore, although recent benchmarks have evaluated various full-duplex interaction capabilities ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026c ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Lin et al., 2026a ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Ray et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2026 ) , the evolution of model behavior and performance over extended, continuous sessions remains insufficiently understood. Our simulations of extended conversations with representative end-to-end full-duplex models reveal a range of failure modes that emerge as interactions progress. These include diminished responsiveness, the production of semantically incoherent utterances, sometimes degenerating into non-speech vocalizations, and noticeable drift in vocal characteristics. To systematically characterize and quantify these phenomena, we propose a simulation-based diagnostic framework that enables dynamic, closed-loop interactions between the model and a virtual user. This framework enables a quantitative assessment of how conversational performance changes over prolonged interactions, focusing on three key dimensions: responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To address these degradation patterns, we propose two complementary approaches that improve long-session stability through training and context management. First, we introduce privileged-context self-distillation, a training framework designed to preserve short-session conversational capabilities over extended interactions without requiring an external full-duplex dialogue corpus. By connecting short sessions into long, coherent conversational trajectories, the framework constructs self-distillation targets. Second, we introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture, which adapts UniGist, an online context compression method ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , to manage growing conversational contexts in streaming full-duplex interaction. In the models we study, dialogue histories accumulate acoustic details and control tokens alongside linguistic content as conversations progress. Some of these details may become less relevant over time. Retaining the entire history at full resolution increases memory costs and may make reliable processing more difficult. TRC therefore preserves recent interactions at full resolution while compressing earlier context into compact KV-cache representations. This design enables memory-efficient streaming inference while remaining well-suited to the proposed training framework. We evaluate the proposed approaches across three full-duplex models with distinct architectures. Our results show that self-distillation mitigates long-session behavioral degradation within the training horizon. Combining self-distillation with TRC reduces degradation in spoken content and voice consistency by 71–96% relative to the baseline across all three models. Crucially, TRC extends these improvements beyond the training horizon, sustaining coherent responses and voice consistency in 20-minute conversations, whereas self-distillation alone exhibits severe behavioral collapse. Moreover, TRC reduces KV-cache growth by 91.7–95.8% . It also limits the increase in backbone inference latency to 12–15% in models with growing context windows, compared with 141–259% without TRC. Together, these results demonstrate that the proposed approaches enable existing full-duplex models to sustain longer conversations with improved behavioral stability and computational efficiency.

sections.heading: 2.1 Full-Duplex Speech Modeling
sections.text: Spoken dialogue systems are commonly characterized by how they coordinate listening and speaking. Half-duplex systems alternate between listening and speaking in separate turns ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2024 ) . Full-duplex systems support concurrent listening and speaking, allowing user input to be processed during an ongoing system response. One approach uses a dedicated turn-taking mechanism to determine whether the system should initiate, continue, or stop speaking. This includes external controllers ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Liao et al., 2025 ) and predictors operating on the dialogue model’s internal representations ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025b ) . Another approach integrates turn-taking into the generative process, modeling both speech content and conversational timing ( Nguyen et al., 2023 ; Défossez et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Within the latter approach, several recent models use temporally structured speech and text histories to determine response timing and produce hidden representations that condition speech generation ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Roy et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . As conversations unfold, linguistic, acoustic, and interaction-related information accumulates into long, heterogeneous histories. These histories can become increasingly difficult for the models to process reliably. When such difficulties arise, their effects may extend beyond recall and response content to speech quality and basic responsiveness, including whether and when the model responds. This motivates our focus on the long-session stability of these models and their ability to sustain reliable spoken interaction.

sections.heading: 2.2 Evaluation of Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Models
sections.text: Existing benchmarks evaluate a broad range of capabilities required for effective full-duplex spoken interaction. Several benchmarks assess conversational timing and dynamics, including turn-taking, interruption handling, backchanneling, and responses to overlapping speech ( Arora et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026c ) . Related evaluations also test whether models can adjust their turn-taking behavior to explicit instructions ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . Beyond interaction dynamics, multi-turn evaluations assess models’ ability to maintain coherent responses, follow instructions, track and update information, and respond safely across conversational turns ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ) . Task-oriented benchmarks further evaluate voice agents’ ability to use tools and complete tasks in interactive environments, alongside the quality of their spoken interactions ( Lin et al., 2026a ; Ray et al., 2026 ; Bogavelli et al., 2026 ; Bhosale et al., 2026 ) . Alongside the breadth of capabilities evaluated, a complementary question concerns how performance changes as a session progresses. Prior analyses have examined this question across conversational rounds and elapsed time, revealing degradation in turn-taking and instruction following ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ) . We extend this line of analysis to longer, dynamically evolving conversations. We also broaden its scope to examine how degradation emerges and progresses across responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency.

sections.heading: 2.3 Streaming Long-Context Modeling
sections.text: Transformer-based models accumulate a key-value (KV) cache as the context grows, increasing memory and computational costs during inference. KV-cache eviction methods reduce these costs by retaining initial and recent tokens or selecting token states according to attention-based importance ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Xiao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Learned compression methods encode context into compact representations. These include reusable KV prefixes for task instructions ( Mu et al., 2023 ) and summary vectors or memory slots for longer contexts ( Chevalier et al., 2023 ; Ge et al., 2024 ) . For contexts that grow incrementally, compression can be integrated into sequential processing through progressive activation compression and online memory updates ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . UniGist combines a local window of raw tokens with accumulated gist representations, allowing older raw tokens to be discarded as the sequence grows ( Deng et al., 2025 ) . These approaches have primarily been studied in text-based language modeling. We build on this line of work to adapt incremental context compression to full-duplex spoken dialogue models that integrate speech generation and conversational timing within a unified generative process.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: We evaluate four end-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models: Moshi ( Défossez et al., 2024 ) , PersonaPlex ( Roy et al., 2026 ) , MiniCPM-o 4.5 ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , and Raon-SpeechChat ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . For each model, we simulate 90 English conversations spanning three personas and ten everyday topics, with three episodes per persona–topic pair, each targeting 600 s. Each conversation follows a closed-loop simulation in which the user’s subsequent responses depend on the model’s generated speech, allowing the interaction to evolve dynamically rather than following a predefined dialogue script. The user simulator consists of a large language model (LLM), text-to-speech (TTS), automatic speech recognition (ASR), and voice activity detection (VAD) modules, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Further details on persona and topic instructions, component choices, prompts, and decoding settings are provided in Appendices A.1 and A.2 . The simulated user follows a consistent conversational policy across all models, waiting until the model finishes speaking before responding, yielding the floor when interrupted, and avoiding artificially generated backchannels or interruptions. We use logical time as the basis for interaction timing, with time advancing according to the duration of processed audio rather than wall-clock time. All timing-related decisions and measurements are based on this logical time axis. This prevents variations in model inference and system processing latency from affecting conversational timing measurements. If the model does not begin responding within the predefined timeout, the simulator rephrases the user’s intent and retries; repeated timeouts terminate the session. Detailed simulation procedures and timing configurations are provided in Appendix A.1 . Figure 1: Closed-loop simulation protocol. Overview of the simulation loop, in which model responses are incorporated into the dialogue context to condition subsequent user turns.

sections.heading: Measures.
sections.text: To characterize how model behavior evolves over a session, we evaluate three aspects of full-duplex interaction: responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. We divide each session into one-minute intervals of logical time and track six metrics. For responsiveness, floor transfer offset (FTO) measures the temporal gap or overlap between the end of the user’s speech and the onset of the model’s response during normal turn-taking. Response timeout (RT) rate captures how often the model fails to begin responding within a predefined timeout, while terminated sessions (TS) rate measures the cumulative proportion of sessions forcibly terminated after three consecutive response timeouts. For spoken content quality, conversation quality (CQ) is a 1–5 LLM-based score assessing the contextual appropriateness and coherence of model responses, while word error rate (WER) compares the model’s native text output with an ASR transcription of its generated speech to assess how faithfully the generated speech reflects the intended text. For voice consistency, speaker similarity (Spk sim) measures how closely the generated voice matches its first-minute reference using speaker embeddings. Detailed metric definitions and scoring procedures are provided in Appendices A.3.1 – A.3.3 . For each one-minute interval, we aggregate available observations across sessions using the same criteria for all models. When a session terminates early, observations collected before termination are retained, while subsequent intervals are excluded from all metrics except cumulative TS rate. To ensure reliable estimates, we report metrics only for intervals with sufficient observations, based on predefined minimum sample thresholds. Detailed aggregation rules and reporting thresholds are provided in Appendices A.3 and A.4 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Long-Session Degradation Patterns
sections.text: Figure 2: Behavioral degradation over long sessions. Each point summarizes a one-minute interval, plotted at its midpoint. The gray band in (f) marks the first minute reserved for speaker enrollment. Shaded regions indicate 95% confidence intervals estimated using 2,000 episode-level cluster bootstrap replicates. Detailed numerical results and accompanying statistics are reported in Appendix A.6 . Figure 2 reveals distinct patterns of performance degradation across all four models as conversations progress. Moshi exhibits gradual declines in conversation quality and speaker similarity, followed by a sharp deterioration in responsiveness toward the end of the session. Its response timeout rate rises from 12.7% at 7–8 min to 70.2% at 8–9 min, with the cumulative terminated session rate reaching 96.7% by 10 min. PersonaPlex and Raon-SpeechChat instead exhibit more pronounced degradation in spoken content quality and voice consistency, although the timing of these changes differs. For PersonaPlex, degradation develops progressively throughout the conversation, whereas for Raon-SpeechChat it becomes prominent during the final two to three minutes. Their mean conversation quality scores decline from 4.90 to 1.08 and from 4.62 to 1.03, respectively, between the first and final minutes, while final-minute WER reaches 97.9% and 98.7%, respectively. MiniCPM-o 4.5 exhibits a contrasting pattern, with degradation concentrated primarily in responsiveness. Its median FTO increases from 0.39 s in the first minute to 1.89 s at 8–9 min, indicating progressively slower turn-taking. The response timeout rate reaches 75.8% in the final minute, and the cumulative terminated session rate reaches 66.7% by 10 min. Despite this decline in responsiveness, mean conversation quality remains above 4 among sessions with valid observations, and speaker similarity remains relatively stable, although WER rises from 2.4% to 15.5%. Taken together, these findings show that long-session stability is a multifaceted challenge, with degradation emerging at different stages and affecting different aspects of conversational behavior across models. Detailed per-minute results and illustrative failure cases are provided in Appendices A.6 and A.7 , respectively.

sections.heading: 4 Methods for Long-Session Stability
sections.text: To address the long-session degradation observed in Section 3.2 , we introduce privileged-context self-distillation , which aims to transfer the base model’s reliable behavior in short interactions to sustained conversations. Since learning over extended interactions also requires efficiently handling growing dialogue histories, we further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions while maintaining access to earlier context. sections.heading: Trajectory construction and distillation setup.
sections.text: To enable long-session adaptation without relying on an external full-duplex dialogue corpus, we build on context distillation ( Snell et al., 2022 ) , using each frozen base model as its own teacher. To obtain reliable teacher predictions, we generate dialogues in short segments, avoiding the degradation observed in long sessions. For each subsequent segment, we append a summary of the preceding conversation to the teacher’s system prompt, preserving relevant information from earlier interactions while keeping the teacher’s context compact. We assess the quality of generated segments and regenerate those that fail to meet our quality criteria before concatenating them into continuous training trajectories. Scenario construction, trajectory generation, quality filtering, and prompts are detailed in Appendices B.4 and B.6 .

sections.heading: Training objective.
sections.text: Full-duplex interaction requires the student to preserve not only response content but also speaking decisions and the representations used for speech generation. We therefore supervise content and control predictions separately while matching the hidden representations supplied to the audio decoder. We divide eligible prediction positions into content and control groups based on the teacher-selected token and corresponding speaking state. Content positions correspond to ordinary text predictions during ongoing speech generation, whereas control positions include speech transitions and native interaction-control tokens. For each group, we minimize the teacher-to-student KL divergence D KL ( q i ∥ p i ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{i}\,\|\,p_{i}) , averaging separately over content and control positions to obtain ℒ KL , cnt \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL,cnt}} and ℒ KL , ctl \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL,ctl}} , respectively. This separation prevents differences in group frequency from determining their relative weights, allowing response content and speaking decisions to be weighted independently. We additionally match the hidden representations supplied to the frozen audio decoder using normalized squared error, denoted by ℒ hid \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{hid}} , to supervise decoder conditioning beyond the token-level KL objectives. sections.heading: 4.2 Two-Resolution Context (TRC) Architecture
sections.text: To support sustained full-duplex interaction, models must preserve fine-grained information from recent speech while efficiently retaining relevant context from earlier exchanges. We therefore introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture by adapting gist-based streaming context compression ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2025 ) , enabling incremental compression of dialogue history as streaming inference proceeds. TRC divides each session into consecutive time intervals of duration Δ \Delta , called tiles, and appends a special token, called a gist token, to each tile. sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate the improvements in long-session stability achieved through privileged-context self-distillation and further examine the role of TRC in sustaining these gains beyond the training horizon. We apply our method to PersonaPlex, MiniCPM-o 4.5, and Raon-SpeechChat, three representative native full-duplex models with distinct architectures and publicly available checkpoints and inference pipelines. We do not separately adapt Moshi because it shares the same backbone architecture as PersonaPlex.

sections.heading: 5.1 Long-Session Stability
sections.text: Table 1 summarizes responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency within the ten-minute training horizon and in extended 20-minute sessions, using the same evaluation protocol of Section 3.1 . We use the same aggregation procedure but report results over two-minute rather than one-minute intervals (Appendix A.3 ). Ours (LoRA) applies privileged-context self-distillation without context compression, whereas Ours (TRC) combines the same training objective with the TRC architecture. Within the ten-minute training horizon, privileged-context self-distillation generally improves stability relative to the base models. For PersonaPlex and Raon-SpeechChat, adaptation substantially reduces the degradation in responsiveness, speech–text consistency, and voice consistency observed in the base models. Conversation quality also improves considerably: at 8–10 minutes, the base-model scores of 1.29 and 1.63 rise to 3.84 and 4.19 with Ours (TRC) for PersonaPlex and Raon-SpeechChat, respectively. For these two models, combining self-distillation with TRC yields larger improvements than LoRA alone on most metrics. The pattern for MiniCPM-o 4.5 is somewhat more limited. Both variants improve late-session performance across metrics relative to the base model, but substantial responsiveness degradation remains despite better preservation of spoken content quality and voice consistency. For MiniCPM-o 4.5, TRC provides no additional benefit over LoRA alone within the training horizon. The pattern changes substantially when sessions extend beyond the training range. With self-distillation through LoRA alone, all three models deteriorate sharply beyond the training horizon. Substantial responsiveness problems persist or worsen, while speech–text consistency deteriorates across all three models, with WERs at 18–20 minutes ranging from 88.7% to 99.6%. For Raon-SpeechChat and MiniCPM-o 4.5, conversation quality falls to 1.06 and 1.00, respectively, indicating that the responses themselves collapse. With TRC, however, this degradation beyond the training range is considerably more gradual. PersonaPlex remains comparatively stable from 10–12 to 18–20 minutes, retaining a conversation quality score of 3.53 at 18–20 minutes. For Raon-SpeechChat, conversation quality declines to 3.29 and WER rises to 44.3% by 18–20 minutes, but these remain better than 1.06 and 99.6% under LoRA alone. MiniCPM-o 4.5 continues to lose responsiveness gradually, yet the responses it does produce remain robust in spoken content quality, with a late conversation quality score of 4.64 and WER of 5.8%. Overall, self-distillation improves long-session stability within the training horizon, although the size of the gains varies by model and architecture. Beyond that horizon, TRC retains more of the gains in spoken content quality and voice consistency than LoRA alone. These results indicate greater behavioral stability in extended sessions. sections.heading: Memory recall.
sections.text: To examine how TRC affects memory recall under high compression, we evaluate each model on a simple memory-recall task constructed from 100 question–answer pairs selected from FictionalQA ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2026 ) , after filtering out pairs unsuitable for spoken dialogue. The task measures how accurately a model recalls information introduced at the beginning of a session, using exact-match accuracy against reference answers. We describe the task construction and evaluation setup in Appendix C.2 . Figure 4 shows how TRC affects recall relative to Base across models and probe distances. Because TRC compresses the context, it generally falls short of the strong short-term recall of Base. In exchange, TRC sustains a consistent level of recall as sessions grow longer, which becomes a comparative advantage on models such as PersonaPlex and Raon-SpeechChat, where Base recall degrades or is lost entirely in long sessions. Future work could add explicit memory tasks to the training objective, which our current method does not include, so that the model matches Base on short-term recall while still retaining information stably over long sessions. As the Raon-SpeechChat results suggest, recall also depends on the compression level, so the optimal balance for each model should be identified while taking into account the trade-off with the gains in long-session stability. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we investigated how the capabilities of full-duplex spoken dialogue models evolve over extended sessions and proposed methods to mitigate their degradation. Using a closed-loop evaluation framework, we tracked changes in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency, revealing that all four evaluated models exhibited degradation in at least one dimension, with distinct patterns and onset times. To address this issue, we introduced privileged-context self-distillation and two-resolution context (TRC) management. Across three model types, self-distillation improved stability within the training horizon, while combining it with TRC better preserved spoken content quality and voice consistency beyond that horizon and substantially reduced KV-cache growth. These findings highlight the importance of tracking and addressing long-session degradation in full-duplex spoken dialogue and demonstrate the potential of leveraging reliable short-session behavior together with efficient context management to support more robust extended interactions.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: We used LLMs in the experimental pipeline to generate simulated user utterances and summaries for teacher trajectories and to evaluate conversation quality, as described in the methods. We did not use LLMs for any other data generation, processing, or evaluation. Generative AI tools also assisted with writing and editing research code and scripts; finding, summarizing, and translating relevant literature; translating and editing manuscript text; refining and editing figures; and drafting portions of the paper. These tools did not materially shape the research ideas or methodology and were not used to design experiments or interpret results. The authors reviewed AI-assisted material before its inclusion, checked suggested references against the original sources, and jointly reviewed and revised translated manuscript text. sections.heading: Word error rate.
sections.text: WER compares the model’s native text output, used as the reference, with an offline ASR transcription of its generated speech. Let ℰ WER ​ ( I ) \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{WER}}(I) denote the episodes with one-minute WER scores included in aggregation within interval I I . For each such episode e e , 𝒮 e ​ ( I ) \mathcal{S}_{e}(I) contains the reference sentences used to compute those scores. Each sentence is assigned by the midpoint of its aligned audio span, without splitting at interval boundaries. The reported WER is WER ⁡ ( I ) = 1 | ℰ WER ​ ( I ) | ​ ∑ e ∈ ℰ WER ​ ( I ) ∑ s ∈ 𝒮 e ​ ( I ) ( Sub e , s + Del e , s + Ins e , s ) ∑ s ∈ 𝒮 e ​ ( I ) N e , s , \mathrm{WER}(I)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{WER}}(I)|}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{WER}}(I)}\frac{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{e}(I)}\bigl(\mathrm{Sub}_{e,s}+\mathrm{Del}_{e,s}+\mathrm{Ins}_{e,s}\bigr)}{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{e}(I)}N_{e,s}}, (6) where N e , s N_{e,s} counts the reconciled reference words in sentence s s of episode e e . Native text is associated with speech segments using fixed timestamp-based rules, with a window extending from 1 s before speech onset to 1 s after offset (3 s lookback for MiniCPM-o 4.5). The associated reference and ASR transcripts are normalized and aligned to obtain sentence-level word-error counts. To accommodate words split across text chunks, spacing differences are reconciled only when removing spaces yields identical character sequences (e.g., “hel lo” and “hello”). In addition, MiniCPM-o 4.5 can generate text ahead of speech, leaving long reference suffixes that may not have been spoken. For each group of speech segments aligned together, we select the native-text prefix ending at a word boundary that minimizes character edit distance to the ASR transcript after removing spaces, favoring the longer prefix in a tie. The reference is truncated only when the remaining suffix contains at least five words and constitutes at least 10% of the original reference. This correction limits distortion from potentially unspoken text, although it may also mask genuine deletion errors. We apply the same fixed rule across all MiniCPM-o 4.5 evaluation conditions, consistent with our focus on within-model comparisons.

sections.heading: A.5 Conversation-Quality Judge Prompt
sections.text: The CQ judge evaluates the model’s spoken content using the scoring rubric in Table 14 and the system prompt in Figure 7 . For 20-minute episodes, the same prompt template is adapted to score 20 one-minute intervals. The judge receives the dialogue grouped into one-minute intervals and returns a separate result for each interval (Figure 8 ). The input includes timestamps and indicates which intervals should be scored. For utterances containing multiple sentences, we estimate each sentence’s start and end times by dividing the utterance duration in proportion to sentence word counts. Each sentence is included in every interval that overlaps its estimated time span. For each scored interval, the output contains a rationale followed by an integer score; both fields are null for intervals not selected for scoring.

sections.heading: B.2 Layer Computation
sections.text: Each gist token starts from the shared learnable embedding and is processed alongside raw tokens through the backbone layers. At each layer, keys and values are computed from the normalized input states. Thus, dialogue information acquired by a gist at one layer becomes available to raw queries through its keys and values at the next layer. sections.heading: Scenarios and split.
sections.text: The training scenarios combine five personas with 20 topics, all distinct from those used in the diagnostic simulation. Three personas encourage the use or recall of earlier dialogue, while the other two emphasize sharing experiences and exploring different perspectives. Two topics are held out for validation, and all trajectories derived from a given scenario remain in the same split.

sections.heading: Segments and privileged summaries.
sections.text: Each trajectory contains five segments. Each segment begins with a user utterance and ends at the first point after 90 s when the model has completed its turn and the next user response is pending, subject to a 150 s limit. After each model turn ends, the user-response delay is resampled uniformly from 0.8–1.5 s, with the response onset aligned to the next processing step. At each segment boundary, a new teacher session is initialized with the base prompt and an LLM-generated summary of the preceding dialogue. Summaries are generated by the same LLM used for the user simulator. The summarizer reads the preceding dialogue rather than earlier summaries and is instructed to retain conversational details and speaker attribution. Summary length is guided by the prompt’s instruction to write concise prose, without imposing a fixed length limit. The summarization prompt is provided in Appendix B.6 . The user simulator also conditions on this summary, together with the dialogue accumulated within the current segment. A 2 s silent interval precedes the new segment’s first user utterance, during which the teacher is forced to listen. Teacher dialogues use the decoding settings in Table 5 , with greedy audio decoding for Raon-SpeechChat.

sections.heading: Trajectory branching.
sections.text: For each model, we generate one initial dialogue per scenario. After segments two and four, each dialogue branches into two independently generated continuations that share the same persona, topic, and dialogue summary. Following the segment termination and branching rules described above, we generated four trajectories per scenario, yielding 400 trajectories per model. Of these, 360 were used for training and 40 for validation. The resulting mean trajectory durations ranged from 8.8 to 9.6 min across models.

sections.heading: Quality filtering.
sections.text: A segment is rejected if the model fails to respond within 3 s after a user utterance ends, repeats a word sequence consecutively over a span of at least 20 words within one utterance, or fails to reach a segment boundary within 150 s. Each segment has at most three attempts. On the final attempt, a speaking decision is forced once per user utterance if the model has produced neither speech nor text within 0.8 s after the utterance ends. Positions at which speaking decisions are forced are excluded from KL supervision. If all three segment attempts fail, generation restarts from the beginning of the dialogue or the most recent branching point. Up to five attempts are allowed from each starting point.

sections.heading: Aligned inputs and targets.
sections.text: For both Ours (TRC) and Ours (LoRA), the student receives the base prompt once and replays recorded native inputs without re-encoding dialogue audio. These audio inputs are represented as codes for PersonaPlex and embeddings for MiniCPM-o 4.5 and Raon-SpeechChat. Teacher prediction and audio-conditioning positions are aligned with the corresponding positions in the student’s continuous trajectory.

sections.heading: Supervision.
sections.text: Table 19 specifies the model-specific assignment rules for the content and control KL losses introduced in Section 4.1 . All three losses are masked from the start of each segment through the processing step containing the onset of the teacher’s spoken response to the first user utterance. Beyond this initial interval, KL supervision excludes positions with forced decisions, whereas hidden-state supervision covers all audio-conditioning positions.

sections.heading: Backbone latency.
sections.text: We measure wall-clock backbone latency at batch size 1 in BF16 on one NVIDIA L40 GPU. Base uses the publicly released backbone implementation, while TRC adds its attention pattern and gist-token computation to the same backbone without loading a trained TRC checkpoint. We use random hidden-state inputs and synthetic KV caches with lengths corresponding to 1, 5, 10, and 20 minutes of interaction. Raw inputs follow each model’s minimum position increment, with one position per 80 ms frame for PersonaPlex, two per 80 ms frame for Raon-SpeechChat, and 13 per 1 s tick for MiniCPM-o 4.5. Timings include backbone forward passes, KV-cache updates, and gist-token computation. Cache preparation and restoration, audio modules, output heads, sampling, and worker scheduling are excluded. For each context length and frame type, we perform two measurement rounds. Before every execution, we restore the corresponding cache to its initial state to keep the workload fixed. Each round begins with warm-up, which continues until Base and TRC have each completed at least 100 executions and their combined warm-up time reaches at least 30 s (90 s for the initial warm-up). We then perform 100 repetitions, measuring Base and TRC once each in random order to reduce the effects of temporal variation in GPU performance. We combine the timing samples according to how often frames with and without gist-token computation occur during inference. PersonaPlex and Raon-SpeechChat compute a gist token once every 12 frames, whereas MiniCPM-o 4.5 does so every tick. Table 2 reports the resulting mean latency at each context length and the range of p95 latencies across the four context lengths.

sections.heading: Materials.
sections.text: We select 100 original question–answer pairs from distinct FictionalQA events ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2026 ) . Each episode uses the source fact as its single needle, the original question as its probe, and the natural answer as its reference. We exclude derivative questions and require an answer of one to three words without digits or an integer from 0 to 99. The answer must occur in the fact but not the question; facts and questions are limited to 30 and 25 words, respectively. The opening, fact, and question are synthesized once with Kokoro-82M and reused across conditions.

sections.heading: Evaluation procedure.
sections.text: After the needle, the main session receives only silence, with the model forced to listen throughout. Retention is evaluated at 0, 5, and 10 minutes from the end of the 20 s input slot containing the needle. To prevent each probe from affecting subsequent evaluations, we run it on a separate copy of the model state at the corresponding evaluation point. Each probe presents the same question and lasts 20 s, including both the question and response. The model is forced to listen until it has processed the entire question, including the processing step containing the end of the question audio. It is then allowed to respond. If no lexical text is generated within the next 2 s, we force speaking for one processing step and then return control to the model. Both Base and TRC use greedy decoding. Scoring uses the model’s native text output generated after the question is complete, rather than an ASR transcript of its speech.

sections.heading: Scoring and reporting.
sections.text: A response is correct if it contains the complete reference answer under the following matching rules. Responses and reference answers are Unicode-normalized and lowercased, with punctuation removed except for internal hyphens and apostrophes. Matching tolerates spaces introduced between streaming chunks (e.g., “Lon don” matches “London”), but does not accept an answer occurring only within a longer word (e.g., “art” in “start”). Integer answers accept both digits and English cardinal forms; no additional answer aliases are used. At each retention distance, accuracy is the proportion of probes answered correctly, with incorrect and unanswered probes counted as errors. sections.heading: Appendix D Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: First, our simulator did not initiate interruptions or backchannels, leaving long-session stability under these forms of user behavior untested. Extending the evaluation to include such behaviors would enable a more comprehensive assessment of full-duplex interaction over long sessions. Second, recall accuracy remained limited under high compression. Future work should explore training objectives that improve the retention and use of specific information, while further examining the trade-off between compression and recall. Third, the limited adaptation data may have biased the models’ native full-duplex behaviors. Future work should investigate whether larger and more diverse adaptation datasets can improve long-session stability while preserving the diversity of these behaviors.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.34991v1 [cs.CL] 26 Oct 2026 Diagnosing and Mitigating Long-Session Degradation in Full-Duplex Speech Models Junho Kim Che Hyun Lee Affiliation: IPAI, Seoul National University (SNU) Department of ECE, SNU Donghun Kang Affiliation: IPAI, Seoul National University (SNU) Department of ECE, SNU Youngho Cho Dongwook Lee Heeseung Kim Sungroh Yoon Affiliation: IPAI, Seoul National University (SNU) Department of ECE, SNU Affiliation: Department of AI, University of Seoul AIIS, ASRI, INMC, and ISRC, SNU Abstract End-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models enable natural, real-time spoken interactions with interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. Prior evaluations have assessed diverse interaction capabilities and identified some degradation patterns across conversational turns. However, how model behavior evolves over extended sessions remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we address this gap by systematically characterizing long-session degradation and developing efficient methods to mitigate it. We introduce a closed-loop evaluation framework for long-session stability and apply it to several publicly available full-duplex speech models, revealing degradation over time in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To mitigate this degradation, we propose a self-distillation-based training framework for lightweight LoRA adaptation that improves long-session stability with a small amount of additional training. We further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions in full detail while compressing older interaction history into key-value representations. We evaluate our methods on three models with distinct architectures, assessing long-session stability, information retention, and computational efficiency. Across all three models, we show that LoRA adaptation mitigates performance degradation over ten-minute sessions, while adding TRC extends these gains beyond the training session length and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%. The project page is available online. 1 1 1 https://kimjunho333.github.io/dmlsd-fdsm/ $\dagger$ $\dagger$ footnotetext: Corresponding authors. 1 Introduction Natural spoken conversation involves dynamic coordination between speakers. A listener may respond before an utterance ends, provide backchannels, or interrupt when necessary, rather than waiting for strictly separated turns. Conventional spoken dialogue systems, however, have largely followed a turn-based interaction scheme in which listening and speaking occur in separate stages. To bridge this gap, recent advances in full-duplex spoken dialogue modeling have enabled models to process incoming speech while simultaneously generating spoken responses ( Nguyen et al., 2023 ; Défossez et al., 2024 ) . Together, these advances support more fluid interactions that better reflect the dynamics of natural human conversation. Recent research has increasingly adopted end-to-end approaches to full-duplex spoken dialogue modeling ( Défossez et al., 2024 ; Roy et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) , with efforts to extend these models beyond natural conversational behaviors to support more sophisticated real-time interaction, including tool use and multimodal perception ( Cui et al., 2026 ; Balam et al., 2026 ) . These developments reflect a broader shift toward interactive assistants that can continuously perceive their surroundings, respond to users as situations unfold, and provide ongoing support during everyday activities or complex tasks. Realizing this vision requires models to sustain reliable interaction over extended periods, rather than merely performing well in isolated exchanges. Despite this growing emphasis on continuous interaction, long-session stability has received limited attention in the development of end-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has explicitly targeted long-session stability in end-to-end full-duplex models through dedicated training strategies or architectural designs. Furthermore, although recent benchmarks have evaluated various full-duplex interaction capabilities ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026c ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Lin et al., 2026a ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Ray et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2026 ) , the evolution of model behavior and performance over extended, continuous sessions remains insufficiently understood. Our simulations of extended conversations with representative end-to-end full-duplex models reveal a range of failure modes that emerge as interactions progress. These include diminished responsiveness, the production of semantically incoherent utterances, sometimes degenerating into non-speech vocalizations, and noticeable drift in vocal characteristics. To systematically characterize and quantify these phenomena, we propose a simulation-based diagnostic framework that enables dynamic, closed-loop interactions between the model and a virtual user. This framework enables a quantitative assessment of how conversational performance changes over prolonged interactions, focusing on three key dimensions: responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To address these degradation patterns, we propose two complementary approaches that improve long-session stability through training and context management. First, we introduce privileged-context self-distillation, a training framework designed to preserve short-session conversational capabilities over extended interactions without requiring an external full-duplex dialogue corpus. By connecting short sessions into long, coherent conversational trajectories, the framework constructs self-distillation targets. Second, we introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture, which adapts UniGist, an online context compression method ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , to manage growing conversational contexts in streaming full-duplex interaction. In the models we study, dialogue histories accumulate acoustic details and control tokens alongside linguistic content as conversations progress. Some of these details may become less relevant over time. Retaining the entire history at full resolution increases memory costs and may make reliable processing more difficult. TRC therefore preserves recent interactions at full resolution while compressing earlier context into compact KV-cache representations. This design enables memory-efficient streaming inference while remaining well-suited to the proposed training framework. We evaluate the proposed approaches across three full-duplex models with distinct architectures. Our results show that self-distillation mitigates long-session behavioral degradation within the training horizon. Combining self-distillation with TRC reduces degradation in spoken content and voice consistency by 71–96% relative to the baseline across all three models. Crucially, TRC extends these improvements beyond the training horizon, sustaining coherent responses and voice consistency in 20-minute conversations, whereas self-distillation alone exhibits severe behavioral collapse. Moreover, TRC reduces KV-cache growth by 91.7–95.8% . It also limits the increase in backbone inference latency to 12–15% in models with growing context windows, compared with 141–259% without TRC. Together, these results demonstrate that the proposed approaches enable existing full-duplex models to sustain longer conversations with improved behavioral stability and computational efficiency. 2 Related Work 2.1 Full-Duplex Speech Modeling Spoken dialogue systems are commonly characterized by how they coordinate listening and speaking. Half-duplex systems alternate between listening and speaking in separate turns ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2024 ) . Full-duplex systems support concurrent listening and speaking, allowing user input to be processed during an ongoing system response. One approach uses a dedicated turn-taking mechanism to determine whether the system should initiate, continue, or stop speaking. This includes external controllers ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Liao et al., 2025 ) and predictors operating on the dialogue model’s internal representations ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025b ) . Another approach integrates turn-taking into the generative process, modeling both speech content and conversational timing ( Nguyen et al., 2023 ; Défossez et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Within the latter approach, several recent models use temporally structured speech and text histories to determine response timing and produce hidden representations that condition speech generation ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Roy et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . As conversations unfold, linguistic, acoustic, and interaction-related information accumulates into long, heterogeneous histories. These histories can become increasingly difficult for the models to process reliably. When such difficulties arise, their effects may extend beyond recall and response content to speech quality and basic responsiveness, including whether and when the model responds. This motivates our focus on the long-session stability of these models and their ability to sustain reliable spoken interaction. 2.2 Evaluation of Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Models Existing benchmarks evaluate a broad range of capabilities required for effective full-duplex spoken interaction. Several benchmarks assess conversational timing and dynamics, including turn-taking, interruption handling, backchanneling, and responses to overlapping speech ( Arora et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026c ) . Related evaluations also test whether models can adjust their turn-taking behavior to explicit instructions ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . Beyond interaction dynamics, multi-turn evaluations assess models’ ability to maintain coherent responses, follow instructions, track and update information, and respond safely across conversational turns ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ) . Task-oriented benchmarks further evaluate voice agents’ ability to use tools and complete tasks in interactive environments, alongside the quality of their spoken interactions ( Lin et al., 2026a ; Ray et al., 2026 ; Bogavelli et al., 2026 ; Bhosale et al., 2026 ) . Alongside the breadth of capabilities evaluated, a complementary question concerns how performance changes as a session progresses. Prior analyses have examined this question across conversational rounds and elapsed time, revealing degradation in turn-taking and instruction following ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ) . We extend this line of analysis to longer, dynamically evolving conversations. We also broaden its scope to examine how degradation emerges and progresses across responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. 2.3 Streaming Long-Context Modeling Transformer-based models accumulate a key-value (KV) cache as the context grows, increasing memory and computational costs during inference. KV-cache eviction methods reduce these costs by retaining initial and recent tokens or selecting token states according to attention-based importance ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Xiao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Learned compression methods encode context into compact representations. These include reusable KV prefixes for task instructions ( Mu et al., 2023 ) and summary vectors or memory slots for longer contexts ( Chevalier et al., 2023 ; Ge et al., 2024 ) . For contexts that grow incrementally, compression can be integrated into sequential processing through progressive activation compression and online memory updates ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . UniGist combines a local window of raw tokens with accumulated gist representations, allowing older raw tokens to be discarded as the sequence grows ( Deng et al., 2025 ) . These approaches have primarily been studied in text-based language modeling. We build on this line of work to adapt incremental context compression to full-duplex spoken dialogue models that integrate speech generation and conversational timing within a unified generative process. 3 Diagnosing Long-Session Degradation 3.1 Protocol and Measures Protocol. We evaluate four end-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models: Moshi ( Défossez et al., 2024 ) , PersonaPlex ( Roy et al., 2026 ) , MiniCPM-o 4.5 ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , and Raon-SpeechChat ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . For each model, we simulate 90 English conversations spanning three personas and ten everyday topics, with three episodes per persona–topic pair, each targeting 600 s. Each conversation follows a closed-loop simulation in which the user’s subsequent responses depend on the model’s generated speech, allowing the interaction to evolve dynamically rather than following a predefined dialogue script. The user simulator consists of a large language model (LLM), text-to-speech (TTS), automatic speech recognition (ASR), and voice activity detection (VAD) modules, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Further details on persona and topic instructions, component choices, prompts, and decoding settings are provided in Appendices A.1 and A.2 . The simulated user follows a consistent conversational policy across all models, waiting until the model finishes speaking before responding, yielding the floor when interrupted, and avoiding artificially generated backchannels or interruptions. We use logical time as the basis for interaction timing, with time advancing according to the duration of processed audio rather than wall-clock time. All timing-related decisions and measurements are based on this logical time axis. This prevents variations in model inference and system processing latency from affecting conversational timing measurements. If the model does not begin responding within the predefined timeout, the simulator rephrases the user’s intent and retries; repeated timeouts terminate the session. Detailed simulation procedures and timing configurations are provided in Appendix A.1 . Figure 1: Closed-loop simulation protocol. To characterize how model behavior evolves over a session, we evaluate three aspects of full-duplex interaction: responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. We divide each session into one-minute intervals of logical time and track six metrics. For responsiveness, floor transfer offset (FTO) measures the temporal gap or overlap between the end of the user’s speech and the onset of the model’s response during normal turn-taking. Response timeout (RT) rate captures how often the model fails to begin responding within a predefined timeout, while terminated sessions (TS) rate measures the cumulative proportion of sessions forcibly terminated after three consecutive response timeouts. For spoken content quality, conversation quality (CQ) is a 1–5 LLM-based score assessing the contextual appropriateness and coherence of model responses, while word error rate (WER) compares the model’s native text output with an ASR transcription of its generated speech to assess how faithfully the generated speech reflects the intended text. For voice consistency, speaker similarity (Spk sim) measures how closely the generated voice matches its first-minute reference using speaker embeddings. Detailed metric definitions and scoring procedures are provided in Appendices A.3.1 – A.3.3 . For each one-minute interval, we aggregate available observations across sessions using the same criteria for all models. When a session terminates early, observations collected before termination are retained, while subsequent intervals are excluded from all metrics except cumulative TS rate. To ensure reliable estimates, we report metrics only for intervals with sufficient observations, based on predefined minimum sample thresholds. Detailed aggregation rules and reporting thresholds are provided in Appendices A.3 and A.4 . 3.2 Long-Session Degradation Patterns Figure 2: Behavioral degradation over long sessions. Shaded regions indicate 95% confidence intervals estimated using 2,000 episode-level cluster bootstrap replicates. Detailed numerical results and accompanying statistics are reported in Appendix A.6 . Figure 2 reveals distinct patterns of performance degradation across all four models as conversations progress. Moshi exhibits gradual declines in conversation quality and speaker similarity, followed by a sharp deterioration in responsiveness toward the end of the session. Its response timeout rate rises from 12.7% at 7–8 min to 70.2% at 8–9 min, with the cumulative terminated session rate reaching 96.7% by 10 min. PersonaPlex and Raon-SpeechChat instead exhibit more pronounced degradation in spoken content quality and voice consistency, although the timing of these changes differs. For PersonaPlex, degradation develops progressively throughout the conversation, whereas for Raon-SpeechChat it becomes prominent during the final two to three minutes. Their mean conversation quality scores decline from 4.90 to 1.08 and from 4.62 to 1.03, respectively, between the first and final minutes, while final-minute WER reaches 97.9% and 98.7%, respectively. MiniCPM-o 4.5 exhibits a contrasting pattern, with degradation concentrated primarily in responsiveness. Its median FTO increases from 0.39 s in the first minute to 1.89 s at 8–9 min, indicating progressively slower turn-taking. The response timeout rate reaches 75.8% in the final minute, and the cumulative terminated session rate reaches 66.7% by 10 min. Despite this decline in responsiveness, mean conversation quality remains above 4 among sessions with valid observations, and speaker similarity remains relatively stable, although WER rises from 2.4% to 15.5%. Taken together, these findings show that long-session stability is a multifaceted challenge, with degradation emerging at different stages and affecting different aspects of conversational behavior across models. Since learning over extended interactions also requires efficiently handling growing dialogue histories, we further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions while maintaining access to earlier context. To examine how TRC affects memory recall under high compression, we evaluate each model on a simple memory-recall task constructed from 100 question–answer pairs selected from FictionalQA ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2026 ) , after filtering out pairs unsuitable for spoken dialogue. The task measures how accurately a model recalls information introduced at the beginning of a session, using exact-match accuracy against reference answers. We describe the task construction and evaluation setup in Appendix C.2 . Figure 4 shows how TRC affects recall relative to Base across models and probe distances. Because TRC compresses the context, it generally falls short of the strong short-term recall of Base. In exchange, TRC sustains a consistent level of recall as sessions grow longer, which becomes a comparative advantage on models such as PersonaPlex and Raon-SpeechChat, where Base recall degrades or is lost entirely in long sessions. Future work could add explicit memory tasks to the training objective, which our current method does not include, so that the model matches Base on short-term recall while still retaining information stably over long sessions. As the Raon-SpeechChat results suggest, recall also depends on the compression level, so the optimal balance for each model should be identified while taking into account the trade-off with the gains in long-session stability. Exact accuracies for all conditions and probe distances are reported in Table 23 . 6 Conclusion In this paper, we investigated how the capabilities of full-duplex spoken dialogue models evolve over extended sessions and proposed methods to mitigate their degradation. Using a closed-loop evaluation framework, we tracked changes in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency, revealing that all four evaluated models exhibited degradation in at least one dimension, with distinct patterns and onset times. To address this issue, we introduced privileged-context self-distillation and two-resolution context (TRC) management. Across three model types, self-distillation improved stability within the training horizon, while combining it with TRC better preserved spoken content quality and voice consistency beyond that horizon and substantially reduced KV-cache growth. These findings highlight the importance of tracking and addressing long-session degradation in full-duplex spoken dialogue and demonstrate the potential of leveraging reliable short-session behavior together with efficient context management to support more robust extended interactions.
